topic: Ted Cruz's Senate hearing on a 'Muslim Brotherhood network in America' and the Democratic boycott
question: Is a Senate hearing into Muslim Brotherhood activity inside the United States legitimate counterterrorism oversight, or religious profiling dressed as oversight?
summary:
At 2:30 p.m. today the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Federal Courts, chaired by Ted Cruz, holds a hearing titled 'Hidden in Plain Sight: Confronting the Muslim Brotherhood Network in America.' All five Democrats on the subcommittee — Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Hirono, Padilla and Welch — are boycotting, calling it a 'political creepshow.' The hearing had been on the calendar since May and was listed as postponed after the May 18 attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego, in which two teenagers with white-supremacist manifestos killed three people.

The right's case is that this is ordinary oversight catching up to reality: Executive Order 14362 started a designation process in November 2025, State and Treasury designated the Lebanese, Jordanian and Egyptian chapters on January 13, 2026, and the House bill to go further is co-led by a Democrat. Behind it sits a real criminal record — the 2008 Holy Land Foundation convictions for funneling roughly $12 million to Hamas.

The left's case is that the American half of the title is unsupported: no U.S. entity has been designated by anyone, and the last time the government publicly named American Muslim groups as terror-linked, a federal judge found it violated their Fifth Amendment rights.

Both sides have receipts, and both trim them.
verdict: On today's checkable facts the critics have the better of it, narrowly: the government's own designations and executive order reach only foreign chapters, and the hearing's title asserts a domestic 'network' that no U.S. legal instrument has established. But the right is not arguing from nothing — the Holy Land convictions, the 1991 memorandum, and a bipartisan designation bill co-led by a Democrat are all real, and the boycott means none of it gets cross-examined. Whether scrutinizing a religious-political movement is oversight or profiling is a question the meter cannot settle.
verificationNote: Executive Order 14362 was read in full from the Federal Register text on govinfo.gov, and the January 2026 designations corroborated in Fox News. The Holy Land co-conspirator rulings are cited to the Middle East Forum — a right-leaning outlet reporting a finding against the government — and to the Georgetown Bridge Initiative on the other side. The San Diego attack is sourced to ADL's review of the manifestos and Wikipedia's casualty list. State.gov returned unreadable output, and judiciary.senate.gov, whitehouse.senate.gov, justice.gov, cair.com and fdd.org all returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching; those items are cited from readable secondary sources and flagged where single-origin.

left.label: A hearing about Americans, built on evidence about foreigners
left.framing: The United States has designated three foreign Brotherhood chapters and zero American ones. A hearing titled 'the Muslim Brotherhood Network in America,' with no Muslim American witness and no dissenting expert, is not oversight of a designated threat — it is the 2011 Peter King hearings with a new name, held ten weeks after a mass shooting at a mosque.
left.strongestPoint: The scope claim is checkable and it holds. EO 14362 names Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt and no American entity; the January 13, 2026 designations covered exactly those three chapters. And the precedent is unflattering: when prosecutors publicly listed CAIR, ISNA and NAIT among 246 unindicted co-conspirators in 2007, a federal judge found it violated their Fifth Amendment rights and the government did not appeal that finding.
left.weakestPoint: The boycott forfeits the cross-examination that would test the witnesses, and 'political creepshow' is a label, not a rebuttal. The framing also omits the halves that cut against it: the same Judge Solis refused to strike NAIT's name, finding 'ample evidence' of a link to Holy Land; the Holy Land convictions are real; and the House designation bill is co-led by a Democrat, which is hard to square with pure scapegoating.

right.label: Designated terror finance did not stop at the water's edge
right.framing: Three Brotherhood chapters are now designated terrorist organizations, a jury convicted an American charity of sending Hamas millions, and the Brotherhood's own 1991 memorandum described its work in North America as destroying Western civilization from within. Asking what that network looks like today is what an oversight subcommittee is for.
right.strongestPoint: The underlying record is not invented. Holy Land Foundation and five of its leaders were convicted in November 2008 of funneling more than $12 million to Hamas, with sentences of 15 to 65 years. The 1991 'Explanatory Memorandum' is a genuine FBI-seized document admitted as a trial exhibit. And the designation push is bipartisan: Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-FL) co-leads the House bill with Mario Díaz-Balart.
right.weakestPoint: The title claims more than the government's own instruments support: no U.S.-based chapter has been designated, and the memorandum that anchors the 'network' theory was expressly not treated by the trial judge as supporting evidence of any conspiracy. The political context is also on the record — a Texas GOP strategist told CNN in April that anti-Muslim messaging is 'solid gold' with primary voters, which is not a counterterrorism rationale.

facts.claim: Executive Order 14362 and the resulting January 2026 designations reach only the Lebanese, Jordanian and Egyptian chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood; no U.S.-based entity has been designated.
facts.evidence: EO 14362 directs a report on 'any Muslim Brotherhood chapters or other subdivisions, including those in Lebanon, Jordan, and Egypt.' Fox News, January 13, 2026: State and Treasury designated the Lebanese, Jordanian and Egyptian chapters; Rubio called them 'the opening actions of an ongoing, sustained effort.' Neither document names an American organization.
facts.explanation: Read directly from the Federal Register text. This is the hinge of the dispute: the hearing's title asserts an American network, while every binding U.S. action to date is extraterritorial. It does not follow that no domestic activity exists — only that none has been legally established.

facts.claim: The Holy Land Foundation and five of its leaders were convicted in November 2008 of funneling more than $12 million to Hamas.
facts.evidence: The 2008 verdict found the foundation guilty of giving 'more than $12 million to support Hamas'; defendants received sentences of between 15 and 65 years. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the convictions in 2011 and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in 2012.
facts.explanation: The strongest fact on the right's side, and it is not seriously contested. Confidence is medium only because the DOJ's own 2008 press release returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching; the figure is cited here from a readable secondary source. Reported totals vary between $12 million and $12.4 million.
facts.source: Wikipedia: Holy Land Foundation for Relief and Development

facts.claim: A federal judge found that publicly naming CAIR, ISNA and NAIT among the Holy Land unindicted co-conspirators violated their Fifth Amendment rights — but refused to remove NAIT's name.
facts.evidence: Judge Jorge Solis found the list 'should never have been released publicly and violated the Fifth Amendment due process rights' of NAIT; prosecutors called it an 'unfortunate oversight.' He nonetheless denied NAIT's request to be struck from the list, finding 'ample evidence' connecting it to Holy Land. The Fifth Circuit ordered the opinion unsealed on October 20, 2010.
facts.explanation: The single most two-sided fact of the day, and each side quotes half of it. Cited to a right-leaning outlet reporting a ruling against the government — the strongest available corroboration. Accounts differ on whether the Fifth Circuit's relief extended beyond NAIT.

facts.claim: The Brotherhood's 1991 'Explanatory Memorandum' is a genuine FBI-seized document admitted as a Holy Land trial exhibit, but the presiding judge did not treat it as evidence of a conspiracy.
facts.evidence: The memorandum describes the Brotherhood's work in America as 'a kind of grand Jihad in eliminating and destroying the Western civilization from within.' It 'was admitted as an exhibit to the court during the 2007 Holy Land Foundation trial.' Per the judge's 2009 opinion, it was not 'supporting evidence' for the money laundering charges 'nor any other conspiracy.'
facts.explanation: Both halves check out, which is why the document sustains two opposite readings. The Middle East Forum notes it was seized from the home of a man prosecutors called the Brotherhood's American 'archivist'; Georgetown's Bridge Initiative notes no evidence it was ever adopted at the 1991 council meeting. Graded mixed because its evidentiary weight, not its existence, is what is in dispute.

facts.claim: All five Democrats on the subcommittee are boycotting the hearing, calling it a 'political creepshow,' and Cruz's office responded 'Of course they are.'
facts.evidence: Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Hirono, Padilla and Welch: 'Scapegoating Muslims may be a Texas Republican strategist's idea of solid gold to whip up their voters, but Democrats have no intention of indulging this political creepshow, particularly after the recent violence targeting places of faith.' A Cruz spokesperson: 'Of course they are.'
facts.explanation: Confirmed in reporting; the senators' own press release returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so the quotes are cited from the outlet that carried them. The 'solid gold' reference is not rhetorical invention — see the next fact.

facts.claim: A Texas Republican strategist told CNN in April 2026 that anti-Muslim campaign messaging is 'solid gold' with the state's primary voters.
facts.evidence: Vinny Minchillo, a Plano-based Republican strategist: 'It is playing as well as anything I have ever seen with Texas Republican voters. It's solid gold.' The same report cites Sen. John Cornyn's ad pledging to fight 'radical Islam' and Rep. Chip Roy's unevidenced claim of Dallas-area 'no-go zones.'
facts.explanation: Read in the syndicated CNN copy, dated April 11, 2026. It establishes the political incentive the Democrats point to; it does not establish that this particular hearing was called for that reason. Another strategist in the same piece predicted the theme would fade in a general election.

corroboration.source: The Hill (context on the designation push)

facts.claim: The hearing was on the calendar in May and listed as postponed; on May 18 two teenagers with white-supremacist manifestos killed three people at the Islamic Center of San Diego.
facts.evidence: Legis1: the subcommittee's page for the hearing, 'previously scheduled for May, continues to list the proceeding as postponed.' ADL on the attackers' manifestos, titled 'The New Crusade: Sons of Tarrant': they embraced the 'Great Replacement,' cast Muslim immigrants as 'invaders,' and called Muslims 'incompatible and hostile to western values.'
facts.explanation: The attack and its ideology are firmly established. The causal link — that the attack is why Cruz postponed — is reported but was not confirmable in a readable primary or committee source, so confidence is medium and the claim is stated as sequence, not cause.

corroboration.source: Wikipedia: 2026 Islamic Center of San Diego shooting

facts.claim: The bill to designate the Muslim Brotherhood globally is bipartisan, co-led in the House by Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-FL).
facts.evidence: Introduced July 15, 2025 by Reps. Mario Díaz-Balart (R-FL) and Jared Moskowitz (D-FL), with a Senate companion from Cruz. Moskowitz: 'The Muslim Brotherhood has a documented history of promoting terrorism against the United States, our allies, and our society.' It directs State to identify all global branches and assess each for FTO designation.
facts.explanation: This cuts against the claim that the entire project is partisan scapegoating — though it also cuts against the hearing's premise, since the bill's operative text is directed at foreign branches, not American organizations. Reporting identifies only one Democratic co-lead.

powerLens.thesis: The power test here is not hypothetical — the exact hearing has been held before with the parties in the same seats, and the exact objection has been made before with the parties reversed. In March 2011 Rep. Peter King held House hearings on radicalization in the American Muslim community; Democrats called it stereotyping and scapegoating, Republicans called it narrow, legitimate oversight of jihadists rather than a faith. Fifteen years later the scripts are word-for-word intact. But Republicans also spent 2023 arguing, correctly, that an FBI memo profiling 'radical-traditionalist Catholics' was religious guilt-by-association — the principle they are now on the other side of.

precedent.what: The House Homeland Security Committee held hearings on 'the extent of radicalization in the American Muslim community.' Rep. Keith Ellison charged King with 'stereotyping and scapegoating'; Rep. Laura Richardson compared him to Joseph McCarthy. Rep. Paul Broun answered: 'The focus of this hearing is not the Islamic religion. It's Islamists. It's jihadists.'
precedent.mirror: Same committee posture, same defense, same objection — down to the boycott logic and the 'we're targeting an ideology, not a faith' rebuttal. What has changed is that the executive branch has since designated three foreign chapters, which gives today's version a legal hook 2011 lacked, and that the hearing follows a mass shooting at a mosque, which 2011 did not.

flips.then: Treated the FBI's 2023 Richmond memo on 'radical-traditionalist Catholic ideology' as proof that government must never infer danger from religious affiliation; the House Judiciary Committee subpoenaed the FBI director over it, and a DOJ inspector general found agents had improperly conflated religious beliefs with terrorism risk.
flips.now: Convene a hearing premised on a religious-political movement operating an unnamed 'network in America,' with no designated U.S. entity to point to — the same inference from affiliation, aimed at a different faith.
flips.source: CBS News (reporting the memo's fate under a Republican FBI director)

flips.then: Backed and still back the designation project in part: Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-FL) co-leads the Muslim Brotherhood Terrorist Designation Act, joined by Democratic cosponsors, and no Democrat has moved to undo the January 2026 designations.
flips.now: Boycott a hearing on the same subject as illegitimate on its face. Note: the two positions are reconcilable — foreign chapters versus American organizations is a real distinction — so this is a tension rather than a documented reversal, and it is stated at that strength.

powerLens.longRun: Strip out which faith is in the frame and a durable American pattern remains: after a shock, Congress convenes a hearing on a religious community's 'network,' the minority calls it profiling, the majority calls it oversight, and the constitutional check arrives years later from a judge rather than from the chamber. That is what happened in 2007-2010 with the co-conspirator list, and in 2023-2024 with the Richmond memo. Whoever holds the gavel next, the durable question is whether Congress can investigate a movement without indicting a faith — and neither party has yet built a rule it would accept when pointed at its own.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Neither side earns a reasoning-honesty bonus for principle: the right's stated rule about religious guilt-by-association would not survive swapping Catholics for Muslims, and the left's boycott sits awkwardly with its own members' support for the designation bill. Both carry it in their weakest point. The needle rests only on today's checkable facts — the scope of the executive order and designations, the court record, and the evidentiary status of the 1991 memorandum.

pattern.thesis: Reading today's hearing as a standalone oversight event misses that it is the federal instalment of a campaign that has been running at state level for over a year, mostly through investigations that opened loudly and closed quietly. The recurring question is not whether any single inquiry is permissible, but what happens to the accusation after the inquiry finds nothing.

campaigns.where: Collin County, Texas — the EPIC City development
campaigns.what: A proposed 402-acre Muslim-led community drew a DOJ civil-rights investigation and multiple Texas state probes. DOJ closed its investigation after developers affirmed the project would comply with the Fair Housing Act; at least three state investigations continued afterward.
campaigns.authorization: Closed without findings (federal); state probes ongoing

campaigns.what: Anti-Muslim themes became a standard primary message — a Cornyn ad on 'radical Islam,' Paxton's charge that Cornyn helped 'radical Islamic Afghans invade Texas,' Rep. Chip Roy's unevidenced 'no-go zones' claim — with a GOP strategist calling the message 'solid gold' with primary voters.

campaigns.where: Executive branch — EO 14362 and the January 2026 designations
campaigns.what: The order set a 30-day reporting and 45-day action clock; State and Treasury designated the Lebanese, Jordanian and Egyptian chapters on January 13, 2026. Career opposition to a blanket designation has been consistent across administrations, with the CIA warning in 2017 that it would 'fuel extremism' given how many regional parties are affiliated.

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is what a cleared investigation is worth. EPIC City was cleared federally and is still under state investigation; CAIR was named, found to have had its rights violated, and is still named. The 'one-off' tell to watch for: an argument that defends this hearing purely on its own terms and never says what finding would count as exoneration.

notAdjudicable: Whether Congress may investigate a religious-political movement at all, or whether the inquiry itself is the injury — a First Amendment judgment about the cost of asking, not a factual dispute.
Whether a boycott is principled refusal to legitimize a proceeding or an abdication of the minority's job to build a counter-record.
Whether the Brotherhood is best understood as a transnational organization or as a family of unrelated national parties sharing a name — a definitional question evidence can inform but not settle.
How much a movement's stated aspirations from 1991 should weigh against the conduct of specific American organizations in 2026.
biasWatch: The bias doing the most work today is the conjunction fallacy dressed as pattern recognition: a story that chains several true facts — a real 1991 document, a real 2008 conviction, a real 2026 designation — feels more probable than any of its links, even though chained claims get less likely, not more. It runs in both directions. On the right it produces an American 'network' no U.S. legal instrument has established; on the left it produces a straight line from a Senate hearing to a mosque shooting. The tell is a narrative in which every fact points the same way and nothing is left unexplained. Real evidence is lumpier than that. A second tell: watch whether anyone's stated rule about religious guilt-by-association survives swapping the faith — the same people who were right about the FBI's Catholic memo are running the hearing, and the same people running the boycott voted for the designations.
